# On the Pleasure of Small Attentions

There's a particular satisfaction in noticing things that don't ask to be noticed. The way condensation forms on a glass in perfect, unhurried rings. The sound a house makes when it settles at night, like it's exhaling after holding its breath all day. The specific shade of green that appears for about ten days in early spring before the leaves commit to their summer color.

I think we spend so much energy looking for meaning in the large events—the milestones, the achievements, the dramatic turns—that we forget meaning was never really about size. A conversation with a stranger that lasts four minutes can rearrange something in you more than a year of routine ever could.

There's also something to be said for the unfinished. The sentence trailing off. The book left at page 200 for three years, then picked up again as if no time passed. We treat incompleteness like a failure, but maybe it's just another shape that things take. Not everything needs resolution to have been worthwhile.

I keep thinking about how strange it is that we're all just walking around with entire interior worlds—full of half-formed thoughts, private jokes with ourselves, songs we hum and forget we're humming—and almost none of it gets shared. Most of what makes up a person never gets witnessed by anyone.

Maybe that's not sad. Maybe it's just the texture of being singular. Or maybe writing, in whatever form, is the attempt to let a little of that interior leak out into the open air.
